title: Leibniz’s Monads — a universe of distinct viewpoints
when: Leibniz developed this mature metaphysics during the late seventeenth century and summarized it in a French manuscript in 1714. He neither published nor titled that manuscript: it appeared in German translation in 1720, while the familiar title was attached to its French edition in 1840.
people: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz; his synthesis drew on Aristotle and Scholastic metaphysics while responding to early-modern mechanists such as Descartes.
origin: Early modern German philosophy, shaped by Leibniz’s work across Leipzig, Paris, and Hanover and by European debates over substance, matter, and motion.
idea: A monad is a simple, indivisible substance, not a tiny physical particle. It has perceptions representing the universe from its own viewpoint, and appetitions—internal tendencies through which it changes. Monads have “no windows”: created things cannot transmit changes into them. Yet their independent changes correspond because God established a pre-established harmony. For Leibniz, bodies and their apparent interactions form a coherent phenomenal order grounded in monads. Perception need not mean conscious thought; many monads perceive only obscurely.
relevance: Leibniz turns the mind–matter problem inside out: instead of explaining how they transmit influence, he accounts for their apparent coordination through harmony. Though contested, his view raises a lasting question: do observed regularities reveal reality’s basic furniture, or only its organized appearances?
